# Stapled Golgi cisternae remain in place as cargo passes through the stack

## Authors

- Gregory Lavieu<sup>1</sup> †
- Hong Zheng<sup>1</sup>
- James E Rothman<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Department of Cell Biology Yale University School of Medicine New Haven United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

10.7554/eLife.00558.001 We have designed a membrane ‘staple’, which consists of membrane-anchored repeats of the trans-aggregating FM domain that face the lumen of the secretory pathway. In the presence of the disaggregating drug these proteins transit the secretory pathway. When the drug is removed these proteins form electron-dense plaques which we term staples. Unexpectedly, when initially positioned within the cis-Golgi, staples remained at the cis face of the Golgi even after many hours. By contrast, soluble FM-aggregates transited the Golgi. Staples and soluble aggregates placed in cis-Golgi cisternae therefore have different fates. Whereas the membrane staples are located in the flattened, stacked central regions of the cisternae, the soluble aggregates are in the dilated rims. This suggests that while the cisternae are static on the time scale of protein traffic, the dilated rims are mobile and progress in the cis → trans direction via a mechanism that we term ‘Rim Progression’. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00558.001

## Introduction

Anterograde transport (cis → trans) through the Golgi stack is a prerequisite for virtually all proteins that are ultimately secreted from the cell, targeted to the cell surface membrane, or localized in a plethora of internal membrane-bound compartments in plants and animals. Despite the fact that this fundamental process was first recognized over 50 years ago, there is still today no general agreement on how it works. The greatest distinction among the competing models for anterograde transport (reviewed in Rothman, 2010) is whether the 4–6 cisternae typically comprising the Golgi stack are proposed to be static or mobile over the time scale of protein flow across the Golgi (typically 5–20 min).

In ‘static’ models, a transport process such as budding/fusing COPI transport vesicles or possibly tubules is required to create anterograde flow of cargo.

In contrast, in ‘mobile’ models, the cisternae themselves continuously move as intact units in the cis → trans direction (termed ‘cisternal progression’), forming at the cis face and being consumed at the trans face, so that no inter-cisternal transport process is required in the anterograde direction. In order to allow the Golgi stack to retain its resident proteins (such as glycosyltransferases) in the face of continuous cisternal turnover, mobile/cisternal progression models also require concomitant retrograde transport (trans → cis or Golgi → ER, or both) of steady-state Golgi resident enzymes, termed ‘cisternal maturation’ (Glick and Malhotra, 1998; Glick and Luini, 2011).

The strongest evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks is that intrinsically large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates (Bonfanti et al., 1998)—which are far too large to be accommodated by COPI transport vesicles—can nonetheless be rapidly transported across the stack. On this basis it has been widely accepted by deductive reasoning, as distinct from direct visualization, that whole cisternae must indeed progress across the stack. This of course does not rule out that parallel processes of COPI vesicular transport (Pelham and Rothman, 2000) and/or tubule-based transport (Trucco et al., 2004) could also occur.

We sought to further test the cisternal progression paradigm by extending the deductive approach from soluble aggregates to aggregates fixed in the membrane, which should behave identically to soluble aggregates according to cisternal progression models. For this purpose, we designed reversible membrane ‘staples’ loosely modeled on the adhesion protein cadherin, which can adhere cells homo-typically. Cadherins consist of tandem repeats of an adhesive unit that binds itself preferentially in trans (Pokutta and Weis, 2007). A similar unit, which additionally is controllable with soluble ligands that can enter cells, is the FKBP mutant termed FM, which according to its crystal packing also interacts in trans (Rollins et al., 2000), with the additional feature that this interaction is disrupted by ligands such as AP21998 even in living cells (Rivera et al., 2000). This suggests that tandem membrane-anchored repeats of FM domains should mimic cadherin in producing a defined structure (staple) that will reversibly adhere intracellular membranes when it faces the cytoplasm, or in the present application produce intra-lumenal adhesions within Golgi cisternae when the FM repeats are lumenally-oriented. To our surprise, we found that luminal staples and compositionally analogous soluble aggregates placed in cis-Golgi cisternae had entirely different fates. Whereas the soluble aggregates were rapidly transported, the membrane staples remained in place.

## Fate of membrane staples introduced into the cis-Golgi cisternae

Temperature blocks have allowed the selective interruption of the secretory pathway in mammalian cells. A classic example is the 20°C temperature block, which slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER → Golgi transport or transport from cis → trans Golgi (Matlin and Simons, 1983). As a result secretory cargoes accumulate in the TGN, from which they can be synchronously released by raising the temperature to the physiological value of 37°C. Temperature blocks in the 15–18°C range slow export of secretory cargo from the ER, but slow anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in limited penetration of the Golgi stack with accumulation in the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) and the cis-most Golgi cisterna or two (Hobman et al., 1992; Balch et al., 1994; Volchuk et al., 2000).

Following an established procedure (Volchuk et al., 2000) we employed a 16°C temperature block to load and accumulate some of the disaggregated CD8lumenal into the cis-Golgi of HeLa cells. Then, continuing at 16°C, we washout the disaggregating drug to allow for membrane staples reformation in the cis-Golgi. Finally, to explore the fate of these staples we raised the temperature to 37°C to allow anterograde transport to resume (Figure 3A). Unless it is explicitly stated to the contrary, all of these experiments were performed in presence of cycloheximide to prevent protein synthesis.

An independent, biochemical test confirmed that the unassembled CD8lumenal had reached the cis-Golgi but not the trans-Golgi at 16°C. Specifically, a portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal is precipitated by Helix Pomatia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a lectin that binds a N-Acetyl-Galactosamine residue that is only added within the cis-Golgi (Roth et al., 1994). In contrast, the lectin Jacalin, which requires trans-Golgi localized modifications for binding (Spicer and Schulte, 1992), did not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although it did at 37°C (Figure 2D).

To explore the fate of the staples when transport is permitted, we first used a surface biotinylation method and immunofluorescence in intact cells to assess the surface exposure of CD8lumenal after release of the temperature block to allow anterograde transport to resume. Surprisingly, the CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C did not reach the surface and was retained in the Golgi as judged by confocal microscopy (Figure 3B,C, lane 2). Golgi retention of the staples is due to controlled aggregation, because this block to transport was removed when the drug was added back, and CD8lumenal (disaggregated) now moves from the Golgi to the plasma membrane (Figure 3B,C, lane 3). Note that except when mentioned otherwise, we used as a loading control 10% of the pellet fraction (insoluble fraction after sonication), which is almost free of soluble disaggregated-CD8lumenal (including the glycosylated-form). Again we attributed the apparent low efficiency of CD8lumenal transport to transient transfection. Cells that respond to the drug show >50% transport efficiency to the PM after 2 hr chase (Figure 3C, lane 3), consistently with the efficiency of transport of regular CD8-GFP (FM4-free) reported previously (Lavieu et al., 2010).

Altogether, the above experiments reveal that membrane staples formed in the first cisterna of the Golgi stack do not move across the stack, even after several hours.

Interestingly, the staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) being excluded from their rims. This could be the consequence of the fixed dimension of the staples, which are too small to fit across a dilated rim (Figure 5D). So, the staples would be expected to preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna.

## Membrane staples are static at every level of the Golgi stack

Because large soluble aggregates such as collagens can move forward rapidly across the stack (Bonfanti et al., 1998) it was unexpected to observe that membrane staples remain fixed in cis-most cisternae. We therefore wanted to see if staples deposited in later Golgi cisternae might also be static. To deposit staples throughout the Golgi stack we allowed CD8lumenal to enter the Golgi at 20°C in the presence of drug to maintain it in the disaggregated state. Then, the drug was removed at 20°C. Surface biotinylation established that staples formed at 20°C remained at the Golgi even after the cells were warmed up to 37°C for 2 hr (Figure 5G), similar to the cis-Golgi staples. Electron microscopy revealed that the staples formed at 20°C were present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna (Figure 5H). This is not surprising because significant back-up of cargo in the stack at 20°C has been previously documented (van Deurs et al., 1988).

The fact that the staples are retained in place at every level of the Golgi stack further emphasizes the static nature of the cisterna on the time scale being studied (5–6 hr) and also rules out the caveat that the apparently stable cis localization of staples at 16°C results from anterograde transport followed by efficient retrieval to the cis cisternae.

To be certain that the very Golgi harboring static staples continued to engage in productive anterograde transport, we measured the rate of efflux of VSV-G from Golgi areas harboring staples as compared to those that did not. We used photo-activatable GFP-tagged VSV-G (PAGFP-VSV-G [Patterson and Lippincott-Schwartz, 2002]) to activate a cohort of protein within a Golgi area to enable us to measure the release of VSV-G from that same Golgi complex. The rate of the release (half-time ∼ 5 min) of PA-GFP-VSV-G from even long-term (4 hr) stapled Golgi was indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi identified with a red-tagged Golgi marker (ST-RFP) (Figure 6B). This observation and the fact that stapled-Golgi remain properly stacked established that stapled-Golgi is fully functional for transport.

Then we asked if Golgi-staples could interfere with the transport of endogenous large cargo. We used Saos-2 cells, which secrete endogenously produced collagen-I. After transfection with GFP-CD8lumenal, Saos-2 cells were incubated at 20°C in the presence of the disaggregating drug, followed by drug removal to allow the positioning of the staples within the Golgi (Figure 6C upper panel, lane 1,2 show the glycosylated form of CD8lumenal). 2 hr after stapling the Golgi membranes, the culture media was removed and cells were incubated at 37°C in the presence of fresh media containing ascorbate to release collagen-I from the ER. After a 2 hr chase the amount of newly secreted collagen-I was determined by TCA precipitation/immunobloting procedure (Figure 6C). Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hr showed 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi (set to 100%). This suggests that, as reported above with for VSV-G, anterograde transport of Collagen-I is not altered when staples are positioned within the Golgi. To rigorously assess if Golgi staples had only minor effect on secretion, we further tested the rate of transport of collagen-I and MMP2, two proteins secreted by Saos-2 cells. The kinetics of secretion for both proteins did not show any robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus was stapled or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Again, this suggests that the amount of staples that is loaded in the Golgi membranes during the re-aggregation procedure does not poison the anterograde transport function of the Golgi.

To further test if Golgi staples interfere with the behavior of Golgi membranes, we assessed the redistribution of Golgi resident enzymes into the ER under BFA treatment (Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1989). Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER was observed whether Golgi staples were present or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). Note that consistently with the moderate disaggregation reported above (44% solubilization in Triton X100), some aggregates remained in the ER (arrows Figure 6—figure supplement 2). These ER-remaining aggregates did not perturb the behavior of the Golgi resident enzymes (Golgi targeting and BFA-redistribution).

Importantly, FRAP experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showed that staples (localized either within the Golgi or within the ER) readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes and do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes; in fact, Golgi-staples diffused only slightly more slowly than disaggregated CD8lumenal at 20°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). This would explain in a satisfying manner why the essential functions of the Golgi (and ER) such as transport and glycosylation are not perturbed by the presence of the staples, since these behave like any cargo or resident protein within the membrane, as further evidenced by the re-distribution of staples (like any other Golgi cargo or resident enzyme) to the ER as a result of BFA treatment.

Retrograde transport is also a major aspect of Golgi function, and it would potentially be of interest to investigate if staples interfere with such function. While we cannot presently rule out this caveat, even if retrograde transport were blocked it would not diminish our conclusion that anterograde transport of both small and large cargo (next section) can occur at normal speeds without movement of cisternae in the stack.

Previously, we found that soluble aggregates that are compositionally similar to the staples (the main difference being that they were not membrane-anchored) rapidly move forward through the Golgi, analogous to collagens (Volchuk et al., 2000). We noted that these soluble aggregates were concentrated at the rims of the Golgi cisternae, analogous to collagens. Given the prima facia contradiction between our current observation of immobile staples and our prior observation of mobile soluble aggregates composed of virtually the same protein, we repeated the earlier studies and compared the fates of soluble aggregates and staples in the same cells.

This would be expected because they share the same homotypic adhesion FM modules. As expected, when the two FM-containing proteins were present in the ER they were efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). On the contrary homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) were efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). This suggests that hetero-aggregates are not formed efficiently within the Golgi cisternae.

## Discussion

Does the presence of staples perturb anterograde transport? On the one hand, because staples freely diffuse like any other membrane constituent it is hard to imagine how a moderate amount of staples would broadly perturb Golgi transport or function such as glycosylation, and there is no positive evidence from our studies that they do so. On the other hand, because they span and link between two sides of the cisterna, it is easy to see why staples should remain in the thin centers of the cisternae, far from the dilated rims (whose width is too great to accommodate the staples) where transport vesicles bud, and also why staples would be sterically excluded from budding COPI or other vesicles if they did occasionally reach a rim, and thus would remain within the cisterna.

With this in mind, our findings can be simply summarized as follows: 1) membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims; and 2) membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.

The obvious explanation of the above is that while the cisternae in the stack (containing staples mainly in their central regions) are static, the rims of cisternae—mainly containing the soluble aggregates—are mobile (at least on the average) in the anterograde direction, a process we term ‘rim progression’.

However, the unique nature of the artificial staples prevents us from definitively concluding that ‘pure maturation’ does not occur in region of the Golgi stacks that are depleted of staples. Although we established by using broad sets of assays that anterograde transport through stapled Golgi is not altered, we cannot rule out that staples introduced, non-obvious, minor side effects on Golgi.

It would be very easy to mis-interpret rim progression as cisternal progression if the only marker being studied is in the rim (Bonfanti et al., 1998). In retrospect, the principal evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks was the mobility of large aggregates like collagens that are located to the rims (Bonfanti et al., 1998). But in retrospect a stricter interpretation of that data would have been to conclude that the ‘at least some portions’ of the cisterna containing the collagen aggregates (i.e., the rims) are mobile, without reaching any conclusion with respect to the rest of the cisterna. A striking feature of the collagen data is that while the majority of the aggregates are indeed rapidly transported, a sizable minority (∼20% [Bonfanti et al., 1998]) remains in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae, consistent with our results and interpretation.

We do not know how the rims of otherwise stable stacks progress, but the most likely possibility would be cycles of fission and fusion that are known to take place in the Golgi (Pfeffer, 2010). Pfeffer has considered how this could be organized in the cis → trans direction by known Rab cascades in the Cisternal Progenitor model, which could well be the basis for the transport of rims dilated with aggregates. We would imagine that after fission a transiently separated rim would nonetheless remain in register in the stack because its membrane would still be engaged in stacking/tethering interactions. Pulse-chase experiments (Volchuk et al., 2000) showed the appearance of detached rims closely-associated with the edges of the stack that transiently appeared during the transport of soluble aggregates (which we termed mega-vesicles at the time). Retention of rims in transit would facilitate orderly rim progression.

To the extent that the bulk of a Golgi stack is static on the time scale of anterograde transport, this reduces the quantitative demand on retrograde transport of Golgi resident proteins and the need for cisternal maturation. In budding yeast, where cisternae generally do not stack, the process of cisternal maturation is well documented, though formal proof that anterograde cargo is present in maturing cisternae is still lacking (Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006). We do not wish to conclude that cisternal maturation does not occur in the stacked Golgi of complex plants and animals, or that it may not be important in re-assembly of the Golgi after cell division, only that it does not appear to be required on the time scale of biosynthetic protein transport in interphase in stacked Golgi.

How are smaller cargoes that do not create dilated rims transported across the Golgi if the cisternae are static? We propose that rim progression is dedicated to large soluble aggregates that due to physical constraints are forced into the rims away from adhesive centers of cisternae, and differs mechanistically from vesicle budding. COPI vesicles are known to bud extensively from the rims of Golgi cisternae at every level and contain–in addition to retrograde-directed cargo–anterograde-directed cargo such as insulin, albumin, and VSV-G (Rothman, 2010); so this biochemically well-understood pathway (Popoff et al., 2011) would seem to be the principal contender. There may well be other, parallel pathways depending on physiological state, specifically budding/fusing tubules, which have been observed especially under conditions of protein over-expression (Ladinsky et al., 1999; Trucco et al., 2004).

Our findings, along with other evidence (Brugger et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 2008), point to a broad division of the Golgi cisternae into two functionally distinct domains: the centers and the rims. The rims specialize in exit and entry into the stack and are dynamic, while the centers are static and adherent to form the stack and specialize in biosynthesis and processing. Much remains to be learned about how these domains segregate and organize the multitude of tasks associated with Golgi function.

## Materials and methods

## Cell culture and transfection

HeLa cells were maintained at 37°C in 5% CO2 in DMEM (Gibco, Grand Island, NY, United States) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco). Saos-2 cells were maintained with the same media supplemented with ascorbate (25 μg/ml). HeLa cells were transfected using lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, Grand Island, NY, United States) as recommended by the manufacturer. Saos-2 cells were transfected using electroporation (Nepa21type II model from Nepa gene, Chiba, Japan).

## Plasmids

CD8lumenal (ss-GFP-FM4-CD8 and ss-DsRed-FM4-CD8) were generated by sequential insertion of GFP (or DsRed), and CD8 encoding sequences into a pC4 ss-FM4 backbone vector (ARIAD), using XbaI/SpeI compatibility and BamH1 restriction site. CD8 was amplified from pC4-CD8-GFP plasmid (Lavieu et al., 2010). A similar strategy was used to create ss-DsRed-FM4hGH and ss-GFP-FM4hGH. PAGFP-VSVG and tsVSVG-GFP were ordered from Addgene. J Rohrer provided ST-RFP. Grasp65 and Golgin97 encoding plasmids were a gift from Y Wang and S Munro, respectively.

## Cell surface biotinylation, TCA precipitation, lectin precipitation, SDS/PAGE and immunoblot analysis

These experiments were performed as described previously (Lavieu et al., 2010) with slight modifications. HeLa cells were grown in six-well plates. All the disaggregation/re-aggregation experiments were performed in HBSS (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco) and 100 μg/ml cycloheximide (Sigma, St Louis, MO, United States). Disaggregating drug (AP21998; ARIAD, Cambridge, MA, United States) was used at 1 μM. 16°C, 20°C, 32°C and 37°C incubations were performed using temperature-controlled incubators.

Briefly, subconfluent HeLa cells were biotinylated in 1 mg/ml EZ-Link Sulfo-NHS-SS Biotin at 4°C for 30 min and washed two times with PBS. After neutralization with 100 mM glycine pH7 at 4°C for 30 min, cells were washed, detached and collected by centrifugation. Pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (1% Triton X-100, 5 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl pH7.4 and 1% protease inhibitor) for 1 hr at 4°C and sonicated (80W, 10 s pulse). The cell lysate was centrifuged, and the supernatant was collected. Samples were incubated with neutravidin agarose resin at 4°C overnight for Biotin-labeled protein precipitation. The neutravidin interacting proteins were eluted with SDS sample buffer from neutravidin pellets. Extracted proteins were first separated in SDS-polyacrylamide gels and then transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes for immunoblotting. After blocking with fat-free milk, the membranes were incubated with appropriate primary antibodies. Primary antibodies were detected by chemiluminescence using horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies. Fluorographs were quantitatively scanned using the NIH image software.

When TCA precipitation was required, 0.1% FBS was used. Chase media was collected and precipitated overnight at 4°C with 10% TCA. After centrifugation TCA pellets were washed with acetone prior to being resuspended in loading buffer and analyzed by immunoblotting blot as described above.

For lectin precipitation, HeLa cells extracts containing CD8lumenal were incubated at 4°C with Jacalin-immobilized lectin (Sigma-Aldrich) or Helix pomatia Gel-HPA-immobilized lectin (EY Laboratories, San Mateo, CA, United States) prior to being processed for immunoblotting as described above. For immunoblotting, we used monoclonal anti-GFP (Roche, Brandford, CT, United States), polyclonal anti-mCherry (Biovision, Milpitas, CA, United States), anti-Collagen-I (SP1.D8 from Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank, Iowa City, IA, United States), and polyclonal anti-MMP2 (Cell Signaling, Boston, MA, United States).

## Confocal imaging

HeLa cells were grown on glass coverslip in 24-well plates. For surface labeling, cells were incubated on ice for an hour with a monoclonal anti-GFP antibody (Roche) prior to being fixed for 10 min with 4% PFA and incubated with an Alexa Fluor 546-coupled antibody. Cells were then processed for confocal microscopy imaging, which was performed in multi-tracking mode on either a Zeiss LSM510 or a Zeiss LSM510 META. Images were analyzed using Zeiss LSM510 software or using ImageJ (co-localization finder plugin). For photo-activation experiments we used a multicolor spinning-disk confocal based on an inverted Olympus microscope (IX-71) and Perkin-Elmer Ultraview system with 5-laser and FRAP/photoactivation. VSVG-PAGFP was photo-activated within the Golgi region (identified by the co-expressed DsRed-tagged protein) at 405 nm (80% laser power) for 5 s. VSVG-PA-GFP was imaged using 488 nm light (10% laser power).

## Electron microscopy

## Sample fixation for regular epon embedding

The cells were fixed in 2.5% gluteraldehyde in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer pH7.4 for 1 hr at room temperature. They were rinsed in sodium cacodylate, scraped and pelleted in 2% agar, then post-fixed in 1% osmium tetroxide for 1 hr, en bloc stained in 2% uranyl acetate in maleate buffer pH5.2 for a further hour, rinsed then dehydrated in an ethanol series and infiltrated with resin (Embed812 Electron Microscopy Science) and baked over night at 60°C. Hardened blocked were cut using a Leica UltraCut UC7, 60 nm sections were collected onto formvar/carbon coated nickel grids and stained using 2% uranyl acetate and lead citrate.

## Sample fixation for immunoelectron microscopy

Samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde/0.1% gluteraldehyde in phosphate buffered saline for 15 min then post-fixed with just 4% PFA in PBS for 1 hr. Cells were scraped and re-suspended in 10% gelatin, then placed in cryoprotectant 2.3 M sucrose overnight at 4°C. These were transferred to aluminum pins and rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen. The frozen block was trimmed on a Leica Cryo-EMUC6UltraCut and 65 nm thin sections were collected. The frozen sections were thawed and collected on grids and floated in PBS ready for immunolabeling.

## Immunolabeling of sections

The grids were placed section side down on drops of 0.1 M ammonium chloride for 10 min to quench untreated aldehyde groups, then blocked for nonspecific binding on 1% fish skin gelatin in PBS for 20 min.

Single labeled grids were incubated on either a primary antibody rabbit anti-Gm130 (Abcam) 1:10, rabbit anti-Clathrin (Millipore) 1:100, mouse anti-GFP (Clontech) 1:50, or rabbit anti-GFP (Invitrogen) 1:100 dilutions for 30 min. Grids were rinsed and placed on protein A gold (PAG) 10 nm (UtrechtUMC) for 30 min. Double labeled grids were incubated with mouse anti-GFP antibody with 5 nm PAG and then the rabbit anti-Clathrin with 10 nm PAG, or rabbit anti-GFP with 10nmPAG and mouse anti-Gm130 with 5 nm PAG. All grids were rinsed in PBS, fixed using 1% gluteraldehyde, then rinsed and transferred to a UA/methylcellulose drop for 10 min. Samples were all viewed on FEI Tencai Biotwin TEM at 80Kv. Images were taken using Morada CCD and iTEM (Olympus) software.

claims.claim: CD8lumenal is a chimeric protein designed as the basic unit of a lumenal membrane staple.

Disaggregated-CD8lumenal shows reduced mobility on SDS-PAGE gel (* upper band)... Jacalin, a lectin that binds galactose residues, exclusively precipitates disaggregated CD8lumenal.

claims.claim: ER-aggregated CD8lumenal forms staples that remain within the ER during their lifetime.
claims.source_text: Together, these results showed that ER-aggregated CD8lumenal forms staples that remain within the ER during their lifetime.

claims.claim: Adding disaggregating drug dissolves a portion of the ER staples and allows disaggregated CD8lumenal to behave as a proper anterograde cargo.
claims.source_text: However, this is a reversible state because adding the disaggregating drug dissolved a portion of the staples and allowed disaggregated CD8lumenal to behave as a proper anterograde cargo that is glycosylated in the Golgi prior to being targeted to the cell surface membrane.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by experiments showing transport and glycosylation upon drug addition.

claims.claim: A 20°C temperature block slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER to Golgi transport or transport from cis to trans Golgi.
claims.source_text: A classic example is the 20°C temperature block, which slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER → Golgi transport or transport from cis → trans Golgi (Matlin and Simons, 1983).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is established methodology in the field, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Temperature blocks in the 15-18°C range slow export of secretory cargo from the ER but slow anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in accumulation in the ERGIC and cis-most Golgi cisterna.
claims.source_text: Temperature blocks in the 15–18°C range slow export of secretory cargo from the ER, but slow anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in limited penetration of the Golgi stack with accumulation in the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) and the cis-most Golgi cisterna or two (Hobman et al., 1992; Balch et al., 1994; Volchuk et al., 2000).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is established methodology supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: A 16°C temperature block was used to load and accumulate disaggregated CD8lumenal into the cis-Golgi of HeLa cells.
claims.source_text: Following an established procedure (Volchuk et al., 2000) we employed a 16°C temperature block to load and accumulate some of the disaggregated CD8lumenal into the cis-Golgi of HeLa cells.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental procedure used to position proteins in specific Golgi compartments.

claims.claim: A portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal is precipitated by Helix Pomatia at 16°C, indicating it has reached the cis-Golgi.
claims.source_text: An independent, biochemical test confirmed that the unassembled CD8lumenal had reached the cis-Golgi but not the trans-Golgi at 16°C. Specifically, a portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal is precipitated by Helix Pomatia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a lectin that binds a N-Acetyl-Galactosamine residue that is only added within the cis-Golgi (Roth et al., 1994).
claims.evidence_reasoning: Lectin precipitation provides biochemical evidence of cis-Golgi localization, based on known glycosylation patterns.

claims.claim: Jacalin did not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C, indicating it had not reached the trans-Golgi.
claims.source_text: In contrast, the lectin Jacalin, which requires trans-Golgi localized modifications for binding (Spicer and Schulte, 1992), did not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although it did at 37°C (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence_reasoning: The absence of Jacalin binding indicates lack of trans-Golgi modifications, confirming cis-Golgi localization.

claims.claim: CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C did not reach the cell surface and was retained in the Golgi.
claims.source_text: Surprisingly, the CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C did not reach the surface and was retained in the Golgi as judged by confocal microscopy (Figure 3B,C, lane 2).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation and immunofluorescence experiments.

claims.claim: Golgi retention of staples is due to controlled aggregation, because adding the drug back removes the transport block.
claims.source_text: Golgi retention of the staples is due to controlled aggregation, because this block to transport was removed when the drug was added back, and CD8lumenal (disaggregated) now moves from the Golgi to the plasma membrane (Figure 3B,C, lane 3).
claims.evidence_reasoning: The reversibility of the retention upon drug addition demonstrates that aggregation is the cause of retention.

claims.claim: Cis- and trans-Golgi fluorescent markers (Grasp65 and Golgin97) can be well discriminated by confocal microscopy.
claims.source_text: We confirmed that co-expressed cis- and trans-Golgi fluorescent markers (Grasp65 and Golgin97, respectively) could be well discriminated by confocal microscopy and the degree of separation quantified with Pearson's coefficient
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantitative colocalization analysis.

claims.claim: Golgi-re-aggregated CD8lumenal shows better co-localization with Grasp65 (cis-Golgi marker) than with Golgin97 (trans-Golgi marker).
claims.source_text: Confocal micrograph showed that Golgi-re-aggregated-CD8lumenal, presumably forming cis-Golgi lumenal staples, showed a better co-localization with Grasp65 (3) than with Golgin97 (2).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and Pearson's coefficient analysis.

claims.claim: Staples are recognized in thin sections as electron dense plaques within Golgi cisternae.
claims.source_text: The staples were recognized in thin sections as electron dense plaques within Golgi cisternae (arrows,
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from electron microscopy.

claims.claim: Staples remain at one face of the Golgi within the first cistern or first two cisternae after 2 or 6 hour chase at 20°C.
claims.source_text: Electron-micrograph showing that the staples (white arrows) remain at one face of the Golgi, within the first cistern (A) or in the first two cisternae (B and C) after 2 or 6 hr chase at 20°C, respectively.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy at multiple time points.

claims.claim: Staples that form flat features are localized at the center of the cisternae, and their topological arrangements prevent them from localizing at the rim of the cisternae.
claims.source_text: Staples that form flat features are localized at the center of the cisternae. Their topological arrangements prevent them from localizing at the rim of the cisternae.
claims.evidence_reasoning: The central localization is observed, and the exclusion from rims is inferred from the structural constraints of the staples.

claims.claim: Clathrin, which labels the trans-Golgi, and staples are at two opposite faces of the Golgi.
claims.source_text: Electron-micrograph showing clathrin (10 nm gold particle), which label the trans-Golgi, and the staples (5 nm gold particles) are at two opposite faces of the Golgi.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by immuno-electron microscopy with dual labeling.

claims.claim: Gm130, a cis Golgi marker, is at the same face as the staples.
claims.source_text: Gm130 (5 nm gold particles), a cis Golgi marker, is at the same face as the staples (10 nm gold particles).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by immuno-electron microscopy with dual labeling.

claims.claim: Staples formed at 20°C do not reach the plasma membrane.
claims.source_text: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation, showing that the staples formed in the medial/trans Golgi do not reach the PM.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments.

claims.claim: Staples formed at 20°C are retained throughout the Golgi and not only at the TGN face.
claims.source_text: Electron micrograph showing that the staples formed at 20°C are actually retained throughout the Golgi and not only at the TGN face.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing staple distribution.

claims.claim: Staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C harbor a cis-glycan signature but not the trans-glycan signature.
claims.source_text: Consistently, lectin-precipitation experiment showed that staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C harbored a cis-glycan signature (precipitated by Helix pomatis) but not the trans-glycan signature (not precipitated by Jacalin)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by lectin precipitation experiments showing differential glycosylation patterns.

claims.claim: Membrane staples formed in the first cisterna of the Golgi stack do not move across the stack, even after several hours.
claims.source_text: Altogether, the above experiments reveal that membrane staples formed in the first cisterna of the Golgi stack do not move across the stack, even after several hours.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by multiple experimental approaches including EM, confocal microscopy, and biochemical assays.

claims.claim: Staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae being excluded from their rims.
claims.source_text: Interestingly, the staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) being excluded from their rims.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from electron microscopy.

claims.claim: The exclusion of staples from rims could be the consequence of the fixed dimension of the staples, which are too small to fit across a dilated rim.
claims.source_text: This could be the consequence of the fixed dimension of the staples, which are too small to fit across a dilated rim (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the structural constraints of staples and rim dimensions.

claims.claim: Staples would be expected to preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna.
claims.source_text: So, the staples would be expected to preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the dimensional constraints and observed localization patterns.

claims.claim: Staples deposited in later Golgi cisternae are also static.
claims.source_text: We therefore wanted to see if staples deposited in later Golgi cisternae might also be static... Surface biotinylation established that staples formed at 20°C remained at the Golgi even after the cells were warmed up to 37°C for 2 hr (Figure 5G), similar to the cis-Golgi staples.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments with staples formed at different Golgi levels.

claims.claim: Staples formed at 20°C were present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna.
claims.source_text: Electron microscopy revealed that the staples formed at 20°C were present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing staple distribution throughout the stack.

claims.claim: The retention of staples at every level of the Golgi stack emphasizes the static nature of the cisterna on the time scale being studied (5-6 hours).
claims.source_text: The fact that the staples are retained in place at every level of the Golgi stack further emphasizes the static nature of the cisterna on the time scale being studied (5–6 hr)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive observation of staple retention at all Golgi levels.

claims.claim: The stable cis localization of staples at 16°C does not result from anterograde transport followed by efficient retrieval to the cis cisternae.
claims.source_text: and also rules out the caveat that the apparently stable cis localization of staples at 16°C results from anterograde transport followed by efficient retrieval to the cis cisternae.
claims.evidence_reasoning: The retention of staples at all levels rules out a retrieval mechanism as an explanation.

claims.claim: VSVG-GFP is targeted to the plasma membrane regardless of the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal within the Golgi.
claims.source_text: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation, showing that VSVG-GFP is targeted to the PM regardless of the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal within the Golgi.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments showing VSVG transport in the presence of staples.

claims.claim: The rate of release of PA-GFP-VSV-G from long-term (4 hour) stapled Golgi is indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi.
claims.source_text: The rate of the release (half-time ∼ 5 min) of PA-GFP-VSV-G from even long-term (4 hr) stapled Golgi was indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi identified with a red-tagged Golgi marker (ST-RFP) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by photoactivation experiments measuring transport kinetics.

claims.claim: Stapled-Golgi remains properly stacked and is fully functional for transport.
claims.source_text: This observation and the fact that stapled-Golgi remain properly stacked established that stapled-Golgi is fully functional for transport.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of structural integrity and functional transport measurements.

claims.claim: Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hours show 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi.
claims.source_text: Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hr showed 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi (set to 100%).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement of collagen secretion in the presence of staples.

claims.claim: Anterograde transport of Collagen-I is not altered when staples are positioned within the Golgi.
claims.source_text: This suggests that, as reported above with for VSV-G, anterograde transport of Collagen-I is not altered when staples are positioned within the Golgi.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the quantitative secretion measurements showing minimal difference.

claims.claim: The kinetics of secretion for collagen-I and MMP2 do not show robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus is stapled or not.
claims.source_text: The kinetics of secretion for both proteins did not show any robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus was stapled or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by time-course experiments measuring secretion rates.

claims.claim: Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER under BFA treatment was observed whether Golgi staples were present or not.
claims.source_text: Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER was observed whether Golgi staples were present or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy showing BFA-induced redistribution.

claims.claim: Staples localized either within the Golgi or within the ER readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes.
claims.source_text: FRAP experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showed that staples (localized either within the Golgi or within the ER) readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments measuring fluorescence recovery.

claims.claim: Staples do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes.
claims.source_text: FRAP experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showed that staples (localized either within the Golgi or within the ER) readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes and do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments comparing diffusion rates.

claims.claim: Golgi-staples diffuse only slightly more slowly than disaggregated CD8lumenal at 20°C.
claims.source_text: in fact, Golgi-staples diffused only slightly more slowly than disaggregated CD8lumenal at 20°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative comparison from FRAP experiments.

claims.claim: The normal diffusion of staples explains why essential functions of the Golgi such as transport and glycosylation are not perturbed by their presence.
claims.source_text: This would explain in a satisfying manner why the essential functions of the Golgi (and ER) such as transport and glycosylation are not perturbed by the presence of the staples, since these behave like any cargo or resident protein within the membrane
claims.evidence_reasoning: This explanation is inferred from the FRAP data showing normal diffusion behavior.

claims.claim: Soluble aggregates compositionally similar to the staples rapidly move forward through the Golgi, analogous to collagens.
claims.source_text: Previously, we found that soluble aggregates that are compositionally similar to the staples (the main difference being that they were not membrane-anchored) rapidly move forward through the Golgi, analogous to collagens (Volchuk et al., 2000).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This refers to previous experimental findings by the authors.

claims.claim: Soluble aggregates are concentrated at the rims of the Golgi cisternae, analogous to collagens.
claims.source_text: We noted that these soluble aggregates were concentrated at the rims of the Golgi cisternae, analogous to collagens.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from electron microscopy studies.

claims.claim: When lumenally-expressed soluble FM4 and membrane-bound FM4 proteins are present in the ER, they are efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts.
claims.source_text: As expected, when the two FM-containing proteins were present in the ER they were efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: When soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins are disaggregated, allowed to leave the ER, and then re-aggregated in the cis-Golgi, the Golgi-modified forms are no longer co-immunoprecipitated.
claims.source_text: However, when these same proteins were disaggregated and allowed to leave the ER and then re-aggregated for 1 hr in the cis-Golgi at 16°C, or even further in the Golgi stack at 20°C, the Golgi-modified forms of these same proteins were no longer co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing lack of interaction in the Golgi.

claims.claim: Homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) are efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C.
claims.source_text: On the contrary homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) were efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing homo-aggregation.

claims.claim: Hetero-aggregates are not formed efficiently within the Golgi cisternae.
claims.source_text: This suggests that hetero-aggregates are not formed efficiently within the Golgi cisternae.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing lack of hetero-aggregation in the Golgi.

claims.claim: Soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins segregate into separate aggregates within the same Golgi area.
claims.source_text: Confocal microscopy independently established that the soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins segregated into separate aggregates within the same Golgi area
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy showing spatial separation.

claims.claim: DsRed-hGH is secreted regardless of its own re-aggregation status or the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal.
claims.source_text: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation and TCA precipitation of the media, showing that DsRed-hGH is secreted regardless of its own re-aggregation status, or the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by biochemical analysis of secreted proteins.

claims.claim: Prior to being secreted, disaggregated and re-aggregated DsRed-hGH are cleaved by furin.
claims.source_text: Prior to being secreted disaggregated and re-aggregated DsRed-hGH are cleaved by furin.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is observed by the appearance of cleaved forms on immunoblots.

claims.claim: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde at 20°C, approximately 75% of the staples remain at the cis-face of the Golgi, whereas approximately 75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the opposite, trans-face of the same Golgi stacks.
claims.source_text: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde through but not exit the Golgi following warm-up to 20°C, ≈75% of the staples, as expected, remain at the cis-face of the Golgi, whereas ≈75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the opposite, trans-face of the same Golgi stacks (Figure 7B and graph).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy analysis.

claims.claim: The anterograde transport process permits large soluble aggregates to be carried forward between cisternae that are immobile.
claims.source_text: We conclude that the anterograde transport process permits large soluble aggregates to be carried forward between cisternae that are immobile.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the differential behavior of soluble aggregates versus membrane staples.

claims.claim: Staples freely diffuse like any other membrane constituent, making it unlikely that a moderate amount would broadly perturb Golgi transport or function.
claims.source_text: On the one hand, because staples freely diffuse like any other membrane constituent it is hard to imagine how a moderate amount of staples would broadly perturb Golgi transport or function such as glycosylation, and there is no positive evidence from our studies that they do so.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This reasoning is based on FRAP data showing normal diffusion and functional assays showing normal transport.

claims.claim: Staples span and link between two sides of the cisterna, explaining why they remain in the thin centers of the cisternae far from the dilated rims.
claims.source_text: On the other hand, because they span and link between two sides of the cisterna, it is easy to see why staples should remain in the thin centers of the cisternae, far from the dilated rims (whose width is too great to accommodate the staples) where transport vesicles bud
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the structural properties of staples and cisternal geometry.

claims.claim: Staples would be sterically excluded from budding COPI or other vesicles if they occasionally reached a rim.
claims.source_text: and also why staples would be sterically excluded from budding COPI or other vesicles if they did occasionally reach a rim, and thus would remain within the cisterna.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the size and structure of staples relative to vesicle dimensions.

claims.claim: Membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims.
claims.source_text: With this in mind, our findings can be simply summarized as follows: 1) membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of multiple experimental observations from EM and confocal microscopy.

claims.claim: Membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
claims.source_text: and 2) membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the key experimental findings from multiple assays.

claims.claim: While the cisternae in the stack are static, the rims of cisternae are mobile in the anterograde direction, a process termed 'rim progression'.
claims.source_text: The obvious explanation of the above is that while the cisternae in the stack (containing staples mainly in their central regions) are static, the rims of cisternae—mainly containing the soluble aggregates—are mobile (at least on the average) in the anterograde direction, a process we term 'rim progression'.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This model is proposed to explain the differential behavior of staples versus soluble aggregates.

claims.claim: The unique nature of the artificial staples prevents definitive conclusion that 'pure maturation' does not occur in regions of the Golgi stacks depleted of staples.
claims.source_text: However, the unique nature of the artificial staples prevents us from definitively concluding that 'pure maturation' does not occur in region of the Golgi stacks that are depleted of staples.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges a limitation in the interpretation due to the artificial nature of the experimental system.

claims.claim: It is possible that staples introduced non-obvious, minor side effects on Golgi, though anterograde transport through stapled Golgi is not altered.
claims.source_text: Although we established by using broad sets of assays that anterograde transport through stapled Golgi is not altered, we cannot rule out that staples introduced, non-obvious, minor side effects on Golgi.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges a potential caveat despite the lack of evidence for major perturbations.

claims.claim: Rim progression could be easily mis-interpreted as cisternal progression if the only marker being studied is in the rim.
claims.source_text: It would be very easy to mis-interpret rim progression as cisternal progression if the only marker being studied is in the rim (Bonfanti et al., 1998).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about potential misinterpretation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The principal evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks was the mobility of large aggregates like collagens that are located to the rims.
claims.source_text: In retrospect, the principal evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks was the mobility of large aggregates like collagens that are located to the rims (Bonfanti et al., 1998).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This summarizes the key evidence from previous literature supporting cisternal progression.

claims.claim: A stricter interpretation of collagen data would conclude that at least some portions of the cisterna containing collagen aggregates (the rims) are mobile, without reaching conclusions about the rest of the cisterna.
claims.source_text: But in retrospect a stricter interpretation of that data would have been to conclude that the 'at least some portions' of the cisterna containing the collagen aggregates (i.e., the rims) are mobile, without reaching any conclusion with respect to the rest of the cisterna.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a reinterpretation of previous data in light of the current findings.

claims.claim: While the majority of collagen aggregates are rapidly transported, a sizable minority (approximately 20%) remains in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae.
claims.source_text: A striking feature of the collagen data is that while the majority of the aggregates are indeed rapidly transported, a sizable minority (∼20% [Bonfanti et al., 1998]) remains in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae, consistent with our results and interpretation.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This observation from previous literature is consistent with the current findings.

claims.claim: The most likely mechanism for rim progression would be cycles of fission and fusion that are known to take place in the Golgi.
claims.source_text: We do not know how the rims of otherwise stable stacks progress, but the most likely possibility would be cycles of fission and fusion that are known to take place in the Golgi (Pfeffer, 2010).

results.result_reasoning: The membrane staple design is well-supported by structural reasoning based on cadherin and FM domain properties (C23-C26), direct EM visualization of electron-dense plaques (C28), quantitative measurements of spacing (C29), and functional validation showing trans-interactions via cytosolic staple controls (C30-C31). The design rationale is sound and experimental characterization is thorough.

Multiple independent lines of evidence demonstrate that ER staples remain static but are reversible: confocal microscopy shows ER localization (C33), drug addition enables transport to plasma membrane (C34), biochemical assays show increased solubility and glycosylation upon disaggregation (C35-C38), and the reversibility is clearly demonstrated (C40). The convergence of imaging and biochemical data strongly supports these claims.

The temperature block methodology is well-established (C41-C42 with multiple citations) and properly applied (C43). Cis-Golgi localization is confirmed by two independent lectin precipitation assays showing cis-specific (Helix Pomatia positive, C44) but not trans-specific (Jacalin negative, C45) glycosylation. Surface biotinylation and confocal microscopy confirm Golgi retention of re-aggregated staples (C46), with reversibility demonstrating aggregation-dependent retention (C47).

The central finding that cis-Golgi staples remain static is supported by multiple orthogonal approaches: confocal colocalization with cis- but not trans-markers (C48-C49), EM showing staples at cis-face after 2-6 hours (C50-C51), immuno-EM with cis-marker Gm130 and trans-marker clathrin confirming opposite localization (C53-C54), and lectin assays showing cis- but not trans-glycosylation after chase (C57). The convergence of imaging, immunolabeling, and biochemical data over extended time periods (up to 6 hours) strongly supports cisternal stability.

EM data directly shows staples localize to flattened cisternal centers and are excluded from dilated rims (C7, C52, C59). The proposed explanation based on dimensional constraints—that staples are too small to span dilated rims—is logical and consistent with the measured staple dimensions (~25 nm, C29) versus rim widths (C60-C61). The spatial segregation is clearly documented and the mechanistic explanation is reasonable.

The extension to staples formed at 20°C demonstrates that retention is not specific to cis-Golgi: surface biotinylation shows no plasma membrane delivery (C55), EM shows retention throughout the stack including trans-cisternae (C56, C63), and the phenomenon persists over 5-6 hours (C64). This rules out retrieval mechanisms (C65) and strengthens the conclusion that cisternae are generally static, not just at the cis-face.

This critical control demonstrates staples don't poison Golgi function: VSV-G transport is unaffected (C66), photoactivation shows normal kinetics (~5 min half-time, C67), collagen-I secretion is 92.5±13% of control (C69-C71), BFA-induced redistribution is normal (C72), and FRAP shows staples diffuse normally without perturbing resident enzymes (C73-C76). The comprehensive functional validation across multiple cargo types and assays strongly supports that staples are inert markers rather than disruptive perturbants.

Multiple lines of evidence demonstrate differential behavior: soluble aggregates transit while membrane staples remain static (C5-C6), soluble aggregates localize to rims (C8, C78), co-IP shows hetero-aggregates form in ER but not Golgi (C79-C82), confocal and EM show spatial segregation (C83), secretion assays confirm soluble aggregate transport (C84-C85), and quantitative EM shows ~75% of soluble aggregates move to trans-face while ~75% of staples remain at cis-face (C86). The convergence of biochemical, imaging, and quantitative data strongly supports this key differential finding.

The rim progression model is proposed to explain how soluble aggregates move while cisternae remain static (C9-C10, C93), with the mechanism attributed to physical constraints forcing large aggregates into mobile rims (C108). While this model is consistent with the data, it remains largely inferential. The authors acknowledge they 'do not know how the rims progress' and propose fission-fusion cycles speculatively (C100-C102). Direct visualization of rim dynamics or additional mechanistic experiments would be needed to elevate this from a plausible model to a supported mechanism.

The broader conclusions about Golgi transport mechanisms are partially supported but contain important caveats. The data clearly show that anterograde transport can occur without cisternal movement (C87, C92), and the reinterpretation of collagen data is logical (C96-C99). However, the authors explicitly acknowledge they cannot definitively rule out cisternal maturation in staple-depleted regions (C94) or exclude minor side effects (C95). The proposed COPI vesicle mechanism for small cargo (C110) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The functional domain model (C112-C113) is well-supported conceptually but would benefit from additional direct evidence of rim dynamics.

Reviewers raise concerns about the collagen secretion experiments, noting 'there is no known cargo of this type' and questioning whether the measurements reflect 'new collagen versus previously secreted collagen.' They request clarification on collagen half-life and proper experimental controls to distinguish newly secreted collagen, indicating uncertainty about whether the data support the claims about normal collagen transport through stapled Golgi.

Reviewers question whether 'stapling results in a dead Golgi' with 'a transient block in traffic at the time of drug addition,' requesting data on collagen half-life compared to staples. They also question co-transfection assumptions, stating 'the experiments assume the cells are co-transfected' and requesting measurement of 'the degree of co-transfection,' indicating uncertainty about whether the Golgi remains fully functional.

Reviewers note that 'some staples may be in cis and others trans' and request this be mentioned in the text. This aligns with the manuscript's acknowledgment that cis-interactions 'cannot be ruled out,' but reviewers want explicit discussion of the heterogeneity in staple localization, indicating this aspect needs clarification.

Reviewers question the interpretation of experiments with soluble and membrane FM proteins, asking 'how much FM protein was actually expressed?' and stating 'a Western blot is needed' because 'a plasmid ratio is given but this isn't particularly helpful in determining the actual protein ratio.' This indicates uncertainty about whether the observed segregation and differential transport reflect physiological conditions or are artifacts of expression levels.

comparisons.notes: Strong disagreement on differential transport of soluble vs membrane aggregates (C79-C86). LLM finds convergent evidence from co-IP, imaging, and quantitative EM sufficient. Peer reviewers question whether expression levels were properly controlled, requesting Western blots to verify protein ratios, indicating the data may not reflect physiological conditions.

Disagreement on collagen secretion data (C69-C71). LLM accepts 92.5±13% secretion as evidence staples don't impair function. Peer reviewers question whether measurements distinguish newly secreted vs previously secreted collagen and request clarification on collagen half-life, indicating uncertainty about experimental validity.

Disagreement on Golgi functionality with staples (C66-C68). LLM finds VSV-G transport and photoactivation kinetics demonstrate normal function. Peer reviewers question whether stapling creates a 'dead Golgi' with transient traffic blocks and request co-transfection efficiency measurements, indicating concerns about experimental interpretation.

Disagreement on cis-Golgi localization specificity (C53-C54). LLM finds immuno-EM with Gm130 (cis) and clathrin (trans) markers clearly demonstrate cis-localization. Peer reviewers note heterogeneity, stating 'some staples may be in cis and others trans' and request explicit discussion of this possibility in the text.
